## Model inputs: scaling, tokens and patches {#sec-ch1}

### Quick recap from LLMs

In an LLM, a token id selects one row of an *embedding table* (one learned row per vocabulary entry), producing a vector of width $d_\text{model}$. That vector enters the *residual stream*, which keeps the same width through every layer; each layer adds the output of an attention sublayer and of a feed-forward sublayer, a small two-layer network applied to each position separately. Normalization and position-encoding choices such as RMSNorm and RoPE are conventions layered on this skeleton, not part of the idea. One more fact carries over: if two runs use different tokenizers, the same text becomes a different number of tokens, so their losses are not comparable.

- **Same idea:** every input unit becomes a $d_\text{model}$-wide vector, and everything downstream works on vectors.
- **Adapted idea:** the table lookup becomes either a lookup of a *bin id* or a learned projection of a *patch* of $P_\text{in}$ real values, which has no table.
- **Time-series-specific idea:** values are *scaled first*, and a mask or time index may ride along.

### Why scaling comes first

Series differ in units and level: one counts thousands, another measures tenths. A fixed vocabulary or one shared projection cannot serve both, so each series is rescaled before it becomes input, and the forecast is mapped back afterward. Reported choices differ (@tbl-scalers). The Lag-Llama paper describes both a mean/variance heuristic and a median/IQR standardization; which one is used is left open here.

| Scaling | Model | Source type |
|---|---|---|
| mean absolute value of the context; zeros stay zero | Chronos [@src-56] | paper |
| standardization plus inverse hyperbolic sine | Chronos-2 [@src-57], TiRex-2 [@src-60] | paper |
| z-score of the series | TiRex [@src-59] | paper |
| statistics from only the first 30% of each series | Moirai 2.0 [@src-62] | paper |
| instance normalization; PatchTST adds the statistics back to its output | PatchTST [@src-64]; Moirai [@src-61] | paper |

: Scalers reported by the papers. No scaler is best in general; each is paired with its own model. {#tbl-scalers}

### Three ways to build input tokens

@fig-tokenization-styles shows all three on the same 12 values.

**Bin tokens (Chronos).** After mean scaling, each value is assigned to one of a fixed set of uniform bins; the paper's vocabulary has 4096 entries including padding and end-of-sequence tokens, covering [−15, +15] in its experiments [@src-56]. The model is then an ordinary language model over these ids. Two limits follow: quantization discards position inside a bin, and the representable range ends at the outer bin centers.

**Patch tokens.** $P_\text{in}$ consecutive values (plus a missing-value mask, and in Chronos-2 a time index) pass through a residual MLP into one $d_\text{model}$ vector [@src-57; @src-58; @src-59]. With stride $S_p$ and the series end-padded, the patch count is $N_p=\lfloor (T_\text{ctx}-P)/S_p\rfloor+2$; without overlap or padding it is $\lfloor T_\text{ctx}/P\rfloor$ [@src-64]. Fewer tokens means cheaper attention. With $N$ tokens, the score matrix has about $N^2$ entries, so total attention interaction work grows as $N^2$, while each token interacts with about $N$ positions. Cutting the token count by a factor $k$ therefore cuts score-matrix entries and total attention interaction work by about $k^2$, and attention interaction work per token by about $k$. This concerns the attention interaction term only, not every component of model FLOPs or wall-clock time. The patch length trades token count against how much each token must encode. Moirai chose patch size by data frequency, which its authors call somewhat heuristic [@src-61]; Moirai 2.0 uses one patch size [@src-62].

**Lag tokens (Lag-Llama).** One token per time step, built from values at chosen lags plus date-time features and summary statistics, then linearly projected [@src-63]. The first token needs a history as long as the largest lag.

![Three input styles for the same 12 values. A bin id indexes an embedding table; a patch goes through a learned projection with no table; a lag token is one time step described by earlier values. Settings are illustrative, and the counts (6 patches, 8 lag tokens) are computed in the worked example.](figures/rendered/fig-tokenization-styles.svg){#fig-tokenization-styles}

### Worked example: one series, three inputs

The 12 illustrative values are 10, 12, 14, 13, 15, 18, 20, 19, 22, 25, 24, 28. Their mean absolute value is $220/12\approx18.33$ (derived), so mean scaling gives 0.55 to 1.53. Cutting an illustrative range [0, 2) into 8 bins gives the ids in @fig-tokenization-styles; mapping each id back to its bin center and rescaling shifts a value by up to about 2.04 (derived), the quantization loss. With $P=4$ and $S_p=2$, $N_p=\lfloor(12-4)/2\rfloor+2=6$, the last patch containing 2 padded steps, versus $\lfloor12/4\rfloor=3$ without overlap. For lags $\{1,2,4\}$, steps 1 to 4 lack a full history, leaving 8 tokens. Finally, with an illustrative $T_\text{ctx}=512$, $P=16$, $S_p=8$: $N_p=64$ patches (32 without overlap), so 8 times fewer tokens, $512^2/64^2=64$ times fewer score entries per head per layer, and 8 times fewer positions for each token to attend to (logical counts for the attention interaction term, not measured cost).

### Check your understanding {#sec-ch1-check}

1. **Quick check.** In a bin-token model, what does a bin id select, and in a patch model what plays that role?
2. **Calculation.** A series has 20 steps. Compute $N_p$ for $P=5$, $S_p=2$ with end padding, and for non-overlapping patches of 5.
3. **Misconception check.** "Chronos treats the series like text, so it can forecast any value." What limit does the bin design impose?
4. **Compare.** Name one thing a lag token and a patch token have in common and one thing that differs.
5. **Explain.** Why does the forecast have to be un-scaled, and why can losses on differently scaled series not be compared directly?
6. **Interview practice.** A colleague proposes doubling the patch length with non-overlapping patches. What happens to token count and score-matrix size, and what can you not conclude about accuracy?
